title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
gist: The American Cancer Society has reversed its 2010 stance and now recommends routine PSA screening for prostate cancer: every two years from 50 to 69 for average-risk men, and from 45 for high-risk men, including all Black men. A positive test triggers a repeat test, then MRI or biomarker testing, before biopsy, and active surveillance for low-risk cancers.

insights.claim: The American Cancer Society now recommends that average-risk men get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, reversing its 2010 guidance, which made no universal recommendation and instead advised shared decision-making.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Broader screening guidelines can raise PSA test, MRI, and biomarker volumes, a tailwind for diagnostics.
insights.locator: In a significant update to its guidelines

insights.claim: Under the new ACS guidance, all Black men, and non-Black men with a close relative diagnosed before 65 or multiple affected relatives, should start yearly PSA testing at 45.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Earlier, annual testing for high-risk groups expands the screened population.
insights.locator: Men considered at high risk due to race

insights.claim: Men aged 70 to 74 should consult their doctor about continuing screening, and men 75 and older are not recommended to be screened.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Sets an upper age bound on the addressable screening population.

insights.claim: The ACS says new evidence since 2010 shows screening saves lives and that advances in case management can avoid the harms of overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The shift rests on better downstream triage, which favors imaging and biomarker tools.

insights.claim: The ACS defines a high PSA as 3 ng/mL or higher under 70 and 6.5 ng/mL or higher at 70 and up, and recommends repeating a high test, then using prostate MRI or a validated biomarker test before biopsy unless suspicion is very high.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Embeds MRI and biomarker tests in the standard pathway, creating structural demand for them.
insights.locator: In the new guidance, the ACS adds guardrails

insights.claim: Active surveillance should be the initial management strategy for men diagnosed with low-risk prostate cancer, since many such cancers never cause harm while treatment risks erectile dysfunction and incontinence.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Moves care toward monitoring over immediate intervention for low-risk cases.
insights.quote: lower-risk findings can be safely managed through careful, active surveillance.
insights.locator: For men diagnosed with prostate cancer

insights.claim: Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in US men, with about 334,000 diagnoses and over 36,320 deaths estimated for 2026.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Sizes the disease burden and the market for screening and treatment.
insights.locator: Prostate cancer is one of the most common

insights.claim: The US Preventive Services Task Force is updating its prostate screening recommendation, but it was recently overhauled by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and its new members are reportedly rife with conflicts of interest.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Uncertain federal guidance (which affects coverage) could diverge from ACS, adding policy risk.
